To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the left aCB is significantly more FA than right; (ii) males have higher FA than females in the bilateral a CB; (iii) the dACC has region-specific asymmetry of GMD: right > left at the lower part (near callosal sulc) and left > right at the upper part (near cingulate sulc); (iv) no sex effect for GMD in dACC.
the asymmetry of FA in aCB and GMD in dACC is region-specific, with a higher left aCB FA and right > left in lower dACC but left > right asymmetry in upper dACC.

the left aCB had higher FA than the right aCB in both groups, while GMD was asymmetric in the dACC with right GMD higher than left GMD in the lower part of dACC and left GMD higher than right GMD in the upper part of dACC.

the asymmetry of dACC is complex and region-specific, and the left aCB has higher FA but lower GMD than the right.
FA asymmetry in the aCB is more robust than GMD asymmetry in the dACC, and both are sex-dependent.
both the left aCB and the upper part of the dACC are more developed in males than in females, while the lower part of the dACL is more developed in females than in males.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the dACC is asymmetrically organized in both white and gray matter.
the left anterior cINGULUm bundle (aCB; also referred to as the cingulum) is more important in cognitive control than the right, and that this asymmetry is more pronounced in males.
the asymmetry in the dACC is not a simple phenomenon but rather a complex one.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dACC shows a pattern of asymmetry of both FA and GMP that is consistent with the previous findings.
the asymmetry of FA in the aCB may not necessarily imply the asymmetry of GMD in its corresponding white matter tracts.
